    AI Overview
    Tax Day for 2026 is Wednesday, April 15, 2026. This is the deadline to file federal income tax returns and pay any taxes owed to the IRS for the 2025 tax year. If you need more time, you can file for an extension by this date to push your filing deadline to October 15, 2026, though any taxes owed are still due on April 15. 
    Key points for Tax Day 2026: 
    • Deadline: Returns must be filed or postmarked by April 15, 2026.
    • Extensions: File Form 4868 for an extension, which gives you until October 15, 2026, to file.
    • Payment: Extensions to file are not extensions to pay. Taxes owed must be paid by April 15 to avoid penalties.
    • Special Considerations: Some areas or taxpayers (e.g., in disaster zones or living abroad) may have different deadlines. 
    Would you like to know about filing for an extension, where to file for free, or how to set up a payment plan if you owe taxes?

    People also ask
    What happens if you don't file taxes by April 15th?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    If you don't file taxes by April 15th, you will likely face a Failure to File penalty of 5% of your unpaid tax liability for each month the return is late, capped at 25%. You will also face interest charges. It is highly advised to file as soon as possible, even if you cannot pay the full amount, to minimize penalties. 
    Key Consequences of Missing the Deadline: 
    • Failure to File Penalty: 5% per month (up to 25%) of the unpaid tax amount, which is generally higher than the failure-to-pay penalty.
    • Failure to Pay Penalty: 0.5% of the unpaid tax amount per month, added to the total.
    • Interest: The IRS charges interest on both the unpaid taxes and the penalties.
    • Delayed Refund: If you are owed a refund, you won't receive it until you file. You have three years to claim it before it becomes property of the Treasury.
    • IRS Substitutes: If you do not file, the IRS may file a "substitute return" on your behalf, which usually results in a higher tax bill because you miss out on deductions and credits. 
    What to Do Now: 
    • File ASAP: File your return as soon as possible to stop the penalty accumulation.
    • File an Extension: If you need more time, you can file for a six-month extension, but this only extends the time to file the paperwork, not to pay the taxes owed.
    • Pay What You Can: Even if you cannot pay in full, file on time to reduce penalties. You can set up payment plans with the IRS. 
    Note: If you are owed a refund, there is typically no penalty for filing late.
